source_title: Current correctional and local detention facility UAS buffers and infrastructure exception
revision_date: Repeal scheduled January 1, 2027 by 2026 Act No. 150
uas_topic: Correctional facilities; detention facilities; notice; infrastructure
regulated_party: Any UAS operator near a state correctional or local detention facility
regulated_activity: Operating within 500 feet horizontally or 250 feet vertically of a covered facility
requirement_type: Written-consent rule with commercial infrastructure notification exception and confiscation exposure
permit_or_approval_required: Written consent, or qualifying notification no more than five days and no less than two hours before each operation
summary: Through December 31, 2026, South Carolina prohibits UAS operation within 500 feet horizontally or 250 feet vertically of a Department of Corrections facility or local detention facility without written consent from the Corrections Director or jail administrator. A federally registered commercial operator is excepted when monitoring, operating, maintaining, enhancing, or assessing repairs to electric, communications, water-conveyance, or transportation infrastructure, but must notify the appropriate official separately for each operation no more than five days and no less than two hours beforehand and provide the FAA registration number. Violations may lead to misdemeanor penalties and aircraft confiscation.

source_title: Act 150 contraband, malicious facility surveillance, weaponization, and seizure provisions
uas_topic: Contraband; malicious surveillance; mapping; thermal and geospatial data; weaponization; seizure
regulated_party: Any person operating, taking off, landing, or possessing a drone with prohibited intent
regulated_activity: Contraband delivery, malicious facility data collection, weaponization, threats, or harm
requirement_type: Felony prohibitions, aircraft seizure, and separate-offense treatment
summary: Beginning January 1, 2027, Act 150 creates felony offenses for operating, taking off, landing, or possessing a drone with intent to deliver contraband to a correctional or detention facility; collect visual, photographic, video, geospatial, thermal, or other sensory information about a military or correctional facility to identify vulnerabilities or for another unlawful purpose; or weaponize the drone or threaten or harm persons or property. Aircraft involved may be seized, retained, transferred, or destroyed after proceedings, subject to an innocent-owner process. The data-collection offense requires the stated malicious or unlawful intent; it is not a general ban on every map or image.

Use configuration control so a field crew cannot inadvertently deploy a prohibited or ambiguous payload.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: Use configuration-controlled payload interfaces and maintain documentation showing the purpose, operating limits, release safeguards, aircraft weight, and approved mission configuration. Avoid buying or fielding attachments whose capability could place an otherwise ordinary mapping aircraft within a weapon, projectile, contraband-delivery, or regulated dispensing provision.

summary: Effective January 1, 2027, a South Carolina municipality, county, or other political subdivision may not enact an ordinance that conflicts with Article 3 or FAA regulations. The act nevertheless preserves local authority to impose reasonable restrictions on drone takeoff and landing sites and on operation on or above public property within the jurisdiction when the subject is not otherwise covered by the article. This is conflict preemption rather than a complete displacement of local UAS rules. Local public-property permission and operating restrictions may therefore remain material even after the statewide act becomes effective.

revision_date: Clarified January 15, 2019; current policy page reviewed 2026-08-02

regulated_party: AEC firms and professionals producing survey or photogrammetric deliverables from UAV data
regulated_activity: UAV scanning, LiDAR, mapping, photography, and photogrammetric surveying
permit_or_approval_required: Professional licensure is required when the work constitutes regulated surveying or photogrammetry; the drone itself is not licensed by the Board
summary: The South Carolina engineering and surveying board states that it regulates professional practice, not drones or other tools, and recognizes scanning, LiDAR, and similar UAV methods as acceptable techniques for Tier A or Tier B surveying. In later official minutes, the Board distinguished taking a photograph from photogrammetry and explained that creating measured, overlapping-image products such as contours constitutes licensed photogrammetric practice. The operator credential and the professional credential therefore address different functions: using a drone does not itself require a Board license, but offering or producing regulated survey or photogrammetric work must be performed within the applicable professional-licensure framework.

summary: SCDOT Local Public Agency required provisions implement the American Security Drone Act and OMB Memorandum M-26-02 for federally funded work. The special provision directs contractors to refrain from purchasing or using UAS manufactured by covered foreign entities within existing fleets for operations, maintenance, or data processing on any federally funded project or grant. It points to the Federal Acquisition Security Council list on SAM.gov and a cleared-drone list. This is a project-funding and contract rule rather than a statewide ban on private commercial ownership, but it can disqualify aircraft, associated services, or processing workflows proposed for covered transportation work.
